front.title: Authorization Evidence and Audit Trail for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens

abstract.t: This specification defines JWT claims for including authorization evidence and audit trail information in OAuth 2.0 access tokens. These claims enable cryptographic proof of user consent, supporting accountability, compliance, and dispute resolution in scenarios where autonomous agents act on behalf of users.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In traditional OAuth 2.0 flows, the Authorization Server records user consent internally, but this information is not typically conveyed to Resource Servers or included in access tokens. For many use cases, this is sufficient. However, emerging scenarios—particularly those involving AI agents acting autonomously on behalf of users—require stronger guarantees about user intent and consent.
This specification addresses the need for:

ul.li: Verifiable consent: Cryptographic proof that a user explicitly authorized a specific operation;
Audit trails: Traceable records linking user intent to system actions;
Dispute resolution: Evidence that can be examined if questions arise about what was authorized;
Regulatory compliance: Documentation required by regulations in finance, healthcare, and other domains.

section.t: This specification defines two JWT claims: evidence for user confirmation records, and audit_trail for semantic traceability metadata.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

section.title: Applicability
section.t: This specification defines general-purpose JWT claims that MAY be used with various OAuth 2.0 authorization flows, including but not limited to:

ul.li: Authorization Code Grant (with or without PAR);
Client Credentials Grant;
Token Exchange ;
Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant.

section.t: Different authorization flows may have different security considerations when using this specification. Implementations SHOULD carefully evaluate the security implications based on their specific deployment scenario.

dl.dd: An explicit action by the user (e.g., clicking "Allow") to approve an authorization request.
The human-readable description of the operation shown to the user during the consent flow.
A cryptographically signed record of user confirmation, including what was displayed and how the user responded.
Metadata that enables tracing from user intent through system interpretation to final authorized action.
The process of translating user intent (e.g., natural language) into concrete system operations.

section.title: The evidence Claim
section.t: The evidence claim contains a record of the user's confirmation action during the authorization process. It is included in access tokens to provide verifiable proof of user consent.

tr.td: Unique identifier for this evidence record. The value SHOULD use a collision-resistant format such as a UUID URN (e.g., "urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6").
Details of the user's confirmation action.
AS signature over the confirmation record.
The text shown to user for confirmation.
How the user confirmed (e.g., button click).
Version of the consent UI used.

section.title: AS Signature
section.t: The as_signature field contains a cryptographic signature from the Authorization Server over the evidence record. This signature:

ul.li: Proves the AS witnessed the user's consent;
Ensures the evidence has not been tampered with;
Enables non-repudiation for dispute resolution.

section.t: The signature MUST be computed over the following fields of the evidence object:

ul.li: user_confirmation (entire object)
session_context (if present)

section.t: The as_signature field itself MUST be excluded from the signature computation. The signature input MUST be constructed using JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined in to ensure deterministic serialization. The signature format MUST be a detached JWS in Compact Serialization using the AS's signing key. In detached Compact Serialization (see RFC 7515 Appendix F), the payload portion is omitted, resulting in the format "header..signature".
Note: In examples throughout this document, the as_signature value is shown in abbreviated form for readability. Actual values MUST use the detached JWS Compact Serialization format described above.

section.title: The audit_trail Claim
section.t: The audit_trail claim provides metadata for semantic traceability, enabling analysis of how user intent was interpreted and translated into authorized operations.

tr.td: Reference to the evidence record by ID.
Degree of interpretation applied (none, low, medium, high).
Reference to the original authorization proposal.

section.title: Semantic Expansion Levels
section.t: The semantic_expansion_level field indicates how much the system interpreted or expanded the user's original intent:

dl.dd: No interpretation; user specified exact parameters.
Minor defaults applied (e.g., default quantity of 1).
Substantial expansion (e.g., multi-step plan derived from goal).

section.title: Minimum Content Guidance
section.t: When the audit_trail claim is included, the evidence_ref field SHOULD be present to link the audit record to its corresponding evidence. Including at least evidence_ref and semantic_expansion_level is RECOMMENDED for meaningful audit capability.

section.title: Audit Trail Purposes
section.t: The evidence and audit trail claims serve several important purposes:

tr.td: Records what the user intended, preventing disputes about authorization scope.
Documents how the system translated intent into operations, showing the reasoning process.
Reveals any expansions or defaults applied, enabling users to understand what was authorized.
Provides timestamped proof that the user reviewed and approved the operation.
Enables post-hoc analysis to determine responsibility for erroneous transactions.

section.title: Evidence Generation
section.t: When issuing an access token with evidence, the AS MUST:

ol.li: Record the exact content displayed to the user during consent;
Capture the user's confirmation action and timestamp;
Include the evidence claim in the access token.

section.title: Storage Requirements
section.t: The AS SHOULD retain evidence records for a configurable period to support:

ul.li: Dispute resolution;
Regulatory compliance;
Audit requests;
Token introspection with evidence details.

section.title: Evidence Verification
section.t: Resource Servers MAY verify the evidence claim by:

ol.li: Extracting the as_signature from the evidence;
Verifying the signature using the AS's public key;
Confirming the displayed_content matches the requested operation;
Checking the timestamp is within acceptable bounds.

section.title: Audit Logging
section.t: Resource Servers SHOULD log evidence information for audit purposes, including:

ul.li: Evidence ID;
User confirmation timestamp;
Displayed content summary;
Operation performed;
Outcome (success/failure).

section.title: Signature Verification
section.t: The AS signature over the evidence fields (id, user_confirmation, and session_context if present) is critical for evidence integrity. Implementations MUST:

ul.li: Use strong cryptographic algorithms (e.g., RS256, ES256);
Protect AS signing keys appropriately;
Rotate keys periodically with proper key management.

section.title: Evidence Tampering
section.t: The evidence claim is protected by the access token's signature. However, the as_signature field provides an additional layer of protection specifically for the user confirmation record.

section.title: Replay Attacks
section.t: Evidence records are bound to specific access tokens. The evidence ID and timestamp help detect attempts to reuse evidence across different authorization contexts.

section.title: Token Size Considerations
section.t: Including evidence and audit_trail claims increases access token size. Implementations SHOULD consider:

ul.li: HTTP header size limits when tokens are passed in Authorization headers;
Using token introspection to retrieve evidence details rather than embedding all data in the token;
Limiting displayed_content length to essential information;
Omitting OPTIONAL fields (session_context, interpretation_notes) when not required.

section.title: Displayed Content
section.t: The displayed_content field may contain sensitive information about the user's intent. Implementations SHOULD:

ul.li: Minimize information in displayed_content to what is necessary;
Avoid including personal data unless required;
Consider encryption for highly sensitive content.

section.title: Evidence Retention
section.t: Evidence records may be subject to data protection regulations. Implementations MUST:

ul.li: Define retention periods appropriate to regulatory requirements;
Provide mechanisms for evidence deletion when required;
Limit access to evidence records to authorized parties.

section.title: JWT Claims Registration
section.t: This specification registers the following claims in the "JSON Web Token Claims" registry:

dl.dd: User confirmation evidence with AS signature for authorization proof and audit purposes.
Semantic traceability metadata linking user intent to authorized operations.
